title: ‘Her mental health deteriorated’: family forced to wait years for autism diagnosis
text:
For Rosalyn, the battle for an official autism diagnosis for her 14-year-old daughter, Imogen, has been intense, deeply frustrating and has lasted five and a half years.
That Rosalyn has three other children who have autism diagnoses meant she was acutely aware of the signs.
Rosalyn, 53, from Trafford, Greater Manchester, who works in the medical profession, was diagnosed aged 39. She noticed her youngest child’s problems with socialising and sensory issues at about the age of eight. “It wasn’t going to be unusual that she might also be autistic. We have a very strong family history of it,” Rosalyn said.
The school had noticed issues and agreed to start collecting information for a referral, which took about 18 months. It was sent off in the hope a diagnosis would be made before Imogen started high school.
Then Trafford Autism and Social Communication Pathway “sat on the referral for a while”, said Rosalyn. There were multidisciplinary meetings to decide if they would accept the referral – which took months. Finally, two years later – on 27 March 2023 – Imogen was accepted on to the waiting list.
“And we waited. And we waited. I kept emailing every few months to say ‘where is she?’ And they would say ‘Oh, it’s a 12-month waiting list’. And then after a year: ‘It’s an 18-month waiting list’. And then: ‘It’s a 24-month waiting list’.
“In this time, her mental health deteriorated. She started struggling with a lot of issues that she wasn’t struggling with at the time she was referred.
“I kept writing. The GP wrote several times. Nothing. The school wrote. Nothing. Eventually, about six months ago, I wrote a very strongly worded email.” Rosalyn then listed all the mental health problems her daughter had developed “particularly in the last 12 months”.
“They eventually agreed to expedite her, after three and a half years. They finally saw her about a week-and-a-half ago. But we haven’t got a result yet,” Rosalyn said
Getting a diagnosis is important, she said. “It is helpful to understand who you are,” Rosalyn said. It also affects the support her daughter can access. “Quite a lot of doors are shut to you if you don’t have a diagnosis,” she added.
In school, Imogen does not have an education health and care plan (EHCP) used to access certain support in school. “If you don’t have a diagnosis, that undermines your evidence,” said Rosalyn. “It’s a catch-22.”
Without a diagnosis, she will not qualify for a disabled students’ allowance, which she will need if she goes to university. Or, should she require it, a personal independence payment. Some support groups “want evidence – the evidence is the diagnosis”, Rosalyn said.
“There is a lot of self-diagnosis now, and I think that is because people cannot access diagnosis. You are simply driving people towards self-diagnosis, which is then creating a health inequality.
“You’ve got wealthy people who can access [private] diagnosis. Great. And they are opening the door to all that diagnosis means. And you have people who can’t afford that never getting a diagnosis.”
Of her daughter, Rosalyn added: “She’s into her GCSEs now. Her mental health has massively deteriorated.” They have a “complex family situation”, she said, and Imogen is dealing with a lot of things “perhaps other kids aren’t dealing with”.
“There’s the circumstances around our family life, I accept that. But I think not having a diagnosis for her, she feels like a fraud. People go ‘Well. Do you have a diagnosis? No? Oh right. OK!’ Some people are very critical of self-diagnosis.
“Most people seeking an autism assessment are doing so because they’ve had years of wondering why they don’t feel like other people. Not because it’s trendy. Nobody wants to be autistic. I don’t want to be; I just am,” Rosalyn said.
Imogen’s siblings were diagnosed far more swiftly, partly because of the way referrals are now dealt with and partly to do with waiting times, Rosalyn said.
“With Imogen – six years younger – it’s become such a battle.
“It’s very distressing. She has a lot of issues around her behaviour, her sensory needs, her inability to socialise. She doesn’t leave the house. She’s 14. She should be out living her best life and she isn’t. And that makes me mad.”
